lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Aguinaldo Ballon | Lesson 10 -- When You Do Not Catch It
lesson.grammar_point: indirect questions for clarifying and checking understanding

listenings.text: My team works in three offices: Singapore, London and Brazil. When we started, our weekly calls were a disaster. The people in London spoke very fast, the people in Singapore were too polite to ask questions, and the people in Brazil said yes to everything. Nobody was lying. They just did not want to interrupt. So we created one rule. After every important decision, one person paraphrases it, starting with: so, what we are saying is. It takes thirty seconds. Since then, we have had almost no misunderstandings about dates or numbers.

Okay, quick update before we jump off. The IC signed off on the deal subject to CPs, so we are basically good to go, but the DSCR came in a bit tight, so the lenders want a DSRA of six months instead of three. Legal is on it. We are targeting financial close by end of Q1, assuming the regulator does not move the goalposts on the tariff reset. If anybody has questions, now is the time, because I have a hard stop in two minutes.

paras: In most international meetings today, the majority of people speaking English are not native speakers. A lawyer from Brazil, an engineer from India and an investor from Japan may all be on the same call, each with a different accent. Research on international teams shows something surprising: native speakers are often the most difficult to understand, because they speak fast, use jargon and assume that everybody catches every word.

The most common problem is not grammar. It is a misunderstanding that nobody notices. One person does not catch a number or a date, feels embarrassed to ask, and the meeting continues. Two weeks later, the team discovers that everybody had a different date in mind. Experts say that the professionals who communicate best are not the ones with perfect English. They are the ones who ask a follow-up question, and who paraphrase what they heard to check it.

There are simple habits that help. Ask the other person to slow down, without apologizing for it. When somebody uses jargon, ask them to clarify it. And at the end of an important point, check your understanding with a sentence like: so, what you are saying is that the deadline will change. Most people are happy to explain. Nobody wants a misunderstanding about a contract.
